questions.q: Why does this lesson say organizations often have sensitive data that has never been classified?
options: Because classification schemes don't apply to spreadsheets or log files
Because that data was never discovered in the first place — nobody knew it existed to classify it
Because classification is legally optional in every jurisdiction
Because sensitive data automatically deletes itself after a set period
questions.explain: The lesson's core point is that you can't classify what you haven't found — old exports, forgotten spreadsheets, backups, and log files often hold sensitive data nobody inventoried.

questions.q: What does pattern or regex-based discovery scanning check for?
options: Whether a column's name contains a sensitive-sounding word
Whether the content of a field matches the shape of sensitive data, such as an SSN-formatted number or a credit-card checksum
Whether a file was created more than a year ago
Whether a table has more than 1,000 rows
questions.explain: Pattern/regex-based scanning inspects actual content for recognizable shapes — SSN-like digit patterns, credit-card checksums, email formats — regardless of how the field is named.

questions.q: What is a key limitation of keyword and metadata-based discovery, per this lesson?
options: It requires reading every single row of every table, making it extremely slow
It can miss sensitive data sitting in a column with an unhelpful or generic name, since it relies on naming conventions rather than content
It only works on image files, never on text or numeric data
It cannot be combined with any other discovery technique
questions.explain: Keyword/metadata-based discovery flags likely sensitive fields by name (like 'ssn' or 'dob') without necessarily checking content, so a generically named column holding sensitive data can be missed.

questions.q: Why does sampling-based statistical scanning pull a representative sample rather than checking every row?
options: Because checking every row is technically impossible for any dataset
To keep the scanning process fast enough to run across an entire organization's data estate on a recurring basis
Because sampling is required by GDPR for all data scans
Because row-by-row scanning always produces false positives
questions.explain: The lesson notes that checking every row at scale can be slow and expensive, so sampling estimates sensitivity from a representative subset to keep discovery practical at scale.

questions.q: Which of the following are named in this lesson as real platforms that ship native sensitive-data-discovery features?
options: Microsoft Purview, AWS Macie, and Google Cloud DLP
Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, and Apple Numbers
GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket
Slack, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams
questions.explain: The lesson names Microsoft Purview, AWS Macie, and Google Cloud DLP as real, named examples of this category of tooling, without claiming specific feature details for any of them.
